near_miss.lead: Coordinated parents and other close kin
near_miss.why_not: Cognate kinship nouns recur, but the Norse passages enumerate baptismal relationships or forbidden degrees; the partners concern cosmic riddles, healing, family complaints or reverence. Ordinary kinship enumeration does not establish an inherited formula.

The Atharvavedic exhortation to concordant speech has no corresponding speech formula in the Norse procedure for testimony about work on holy days; retrieval brings together unrelated verbal and nominal derivatives.

The cognate ale noun is real, but the Latvian drinking invitation and its ice/honey comparisons are absent from the Norse Christmas gathering. One beverage word in its expected setting is insufficient.

Norse sofnaði/sofit and Greek hypnos or Sanskrit suptā share the sleep root. Greek waking from a divine dream, Norse interrupted sleep before liturgical singing, and the inferred resting place of Sītā do not share a distinctive syntactic formula. Searches for hypnos plus egeirō returned ordinary waking expressions (Il. 10.159, 2.41, 5.413; Od. 15.44) and later medical prose. The singing/divine-voice comparison in BS-2b0d0 is not a shared collocation with sleep.

The Norse rumour flies, but the assigned Thucydidean passage is about resources for war. Searches for epos plus pteroeis found the Homeric winged-words formula (e.g. Il. 1.201), and epos plus petomai found late discussion of it. Neither word in the Norse flying-rumour expression supplies the corresponding cognate pair, and rumour dissemination differs from the Homeric speech introduction.

The ordered three cognate nouns are striking. Norse prohibits intercourse with actual relatives; MBh 13.132.23 uses three -vat comparisons for treating other men’s wives. Search for all three Sanskrit lemmas returned this witness only. The exhaustive basic female-kin triad is readily recreated, while Christian canon-law transmission offers an alternative to PIE continuity. Insufficient distinctive inherited syntax to claim.

The Norse verse personifies a sword, but its Latin bundle partner is a recipe. Searches for bíta confirm sword/edge biting in other Norse texts; Greek daknō results include figurative pain and Septem 399, but no matched cognate sword-biting formula. Latin mordeo results concern snakes, kissing or spinning. Root searches supplied no stronger cross-branch witness. The poetic motif alone cannot satisfy the anchoring rule.

near_miss.lead: Birth of a son followed by naming
near_miss.why_not: The Irish forms mbert/beirid are forms of beirid, with mac as object; Norse barn is the noun child and the birth verb in preceding context is ól. Irish ainm and Norse nefndr share the name root, but their naming constructions differ. Greek name-plus-tithēmi searches found Od. 18.5, 19.403, 19.406 and Hymn to Demeter 122; these do not restore a shared verbal pair in the slab. Routine birth-and-naming sequence, not a demonstrated inherited phrase.

near_miss.lead: Lying at night with a company
near_miss.why_not: Norse lágo and Old Russian лежащю are cognate, as are nætr and нощь. But nightly military encampment and a particular overnight stay use ordinary locational language; there is no distinctive epithet, figure or fixed wording beyond lying at night.

near_miss.lead: Bearing fire or blood in martial and ritual settings
near_miss.why_not: The skaldic fire vocabulary belongs to a weapon kenning, not a literal offering of fuel. Rigvedic bearing fuel or an offering, Scythian blood poured on a sword, and the Norse relic fire ordeal have different predicates, objects and purposes. No common cognate collocation survives these contextual distinctions.

near_miss.lead: Woman grinding and singing before a king
near_miss.why_not: Search for Greek mylē found Od. 20.105–111 and 7.103–104: women grinding, including an omen-bearing speech by a mill woman. Norse kona and Greek gynē are cognate; Norse mól and Greek mylē belong to the grinding family. Nevertheless the woman’s beautiful singing leading to a sexual encounter differs from a spoken omen to Odysseus, and the shared household activity is too generic. No distinctive inherited phrase; the assigned Irish partners do not improve it.

Norse describes literal mutilation with tongs. Sanskrit describes a warrior as a lion with a sword for tongue and demons with blazing tongues and sharp fangs. The tongue cognate is real, but tongs versus fangs does not establish matching syntax or poetic imagery. Not a shared formula.
